stem: Muscarinic receptors:

options.A: M1 activation decreases potassium flux in the neuron
options.B: M1 activation decreases gastric acid synthesis

reason:
“M1 activation decreases potassium flux in the neuron” seems most correct
M1 ('neural') - found in CNS/PNS/gastric parietal cells. Act via inositol phophate pathway and exert excitatory effects. DECREASE K+ conductance, causing membrane depolarisation
M2 ('cardiac) found in cardiac atria and conducting tissue. Also presynaptic terminals. Inhibit adenylate cyclase, exerts inhibitory effects w/ INCREASE K+ conductance and inhibit Ca2+ channels
M3 'glandular' - found in smooth muscle, vascular endothelium and glandular tissue. Act via inositol phosphate pathway (ie DECREASE K+ conductance). May also cause vasodilation via NO
References

Source Training in anaesthesia - the essential curriculum OST

stem: Which of the following is not an effect of acetylcholine?
reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Acetylcholine stimulates M3 receptors on gastric parietal cells and increases gastric acid secretion, so decreased gastric acid production is not an effect. It also decreases heart rate and AV nodal conduction, causes endothelium-dependent vasodilation, and produces bronchoconstriction. Rang & Dale, pp. 402–403, identifies acetylcholine as a gastric acid secretagogue.

stem: How is adrenaline different to noradrenaline?

reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Adrenaline is produced from noradrenaline by phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase, which adds an N-methyl group (Kam & Power, p.416). Both catecholamines are metabolised by MAO and COMT. Noradrenaline, not adrenaline, is the usual postganglionic sympathetic transmitter, while preganglionic fibres to the adrenal medulla release acetylcholine. stem: In Torsades de Pointes:

options.A: More likely in bradycardia in susceptible individuals

reason:
Reason updated by acolyte on 28/2/2019.

Torsades de Pointes
A polymorphic VT
Associated with prolonged QT.
The definition also requires that the QT interval be increased markedly (often to ≥600 msec). Cases of polymorphous ventricular tachycardia in which the QT interval is not prolonged are treated as generic ventricular tachycardia. Torsade usually occurs in bursts that are not sustained; thus, the rhythm strip usually shows the patient's baseline QT prolongation.

A variety of changes in ionic current can result in the common effect of decreased repolarizing current, reflected in a long QT, and these changes can secondarily lead to subsequent depolarizing currents and sometimes action potentials, termed afterdepolarizations. This leads to a further delay in repolarization and causes early afterdepolarization (EAD), the triggering event for torsade.Phase 3 of repolarization is mediated by activation of the delayed rectifier potassium current (IK) moving outward while the inward positive current decays. If a slow inactivation of the Ca++ and Na+ currents occurs, this inward "window" current can cause single or repetitive depolarization during phases 2 and 3 (ie, EADs). These EADs appear as pathologic U waves on a surface ECG, and, when they reach a threshold, they may trigger ventricular tachyarrhythmias.

These changes in repolarization do not occur in all myocardial cells. The deep endocardial region and midmyocardial layer (composed of M cells) of the ventricle are more prone to prolongation of repolarization and EADs because they have a less-rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr), while other regions might have short or normal cycles. This heterogeneity of repolarization in the myocardial cells promotes the spread of triggered activity, which is initiated by EADs by a reentrant mechanism and currently is thought to be responsible for the maintenance of torsade.

stem: Please see graph below. The dashed line labelled C indicates the baseline vascular function curve for a healthy 70kg adult. After a rapid transfusion of 500ml whole blood, which line will the curve most resemble?
reason: Venous return = (Pmsf - Pra) / resistance to venous return, so on this plot the x-intercept IS the mean systemic filling pressure and the slope is -1/RVR. A whole-blood transfusion adds stressed volume without altering vessel calibre, so Pmsf rises (roughly 3 mmHg for 500 mL at a systemic vascular compliance of about 150 mL/mmHg) while RVR is unchanged. The curve therefore translates to the RIGHT parallel to baseline - line A. Lines that rotate (B, E) involve a resistance change that a transfusion does not cause, and D is a left shift, i.e. volume loss. Note on the source: Pappano & Wier plot this curve transposed (right atrial pressure on the ordinate), where the slope reads as -RVR instead; the plate here uses the Guyton orientation used in ANZCA teaching. The size of the shifts is exaggerated for legibility - direction, parallelism and change of slope are what is being tested.

stem: Please see graph above. The dashed line labelled C is the vascular function curve for a 70kg adult. Which line will the vascular function curve most resemble after a bolus dose of PHENTOLAMINE?
reason: Venous return = (Pmsf - Pra) / resistance to venous return, so on this plot the x-intercept IS the mean systemic filling pressure and the slope is -1/RVR. Phentolamine is a non-selective alpha antagonist, so it does two things at once: it dilates capacitance veins (unstressed volume up, so Pmsf FALLS - a left shift) and it dilates arterioles (RVR falls, so the limb gets STEEPER). Only line B carries both signatures. D shifts left without the slope change, E changes the slope in the wrong direction, and A is a volume load. Note on the source: Pappano & Wier plot this curve transposed (right atrial pressure on the ordinate), where the slope reads as -RVR instead; the plate here uses the Guyton orientation used in ANZCA teaching. The size of the shifts is exaggerated for legibility - direction, parallelism and change of slope are what is being tested.

Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Quiet standing creates high hydrostatic lower-limb venous pressure. Taking a step activates the skeletal-muscle venous pump; competent valves direct blood proximally and interrupt the hydrostatic column, producing the greatest fall in femoral venous pressure. Deep inspiration does not cause a comparable fall and may increase lower-limb venous pressure through increased intra-abdominal pressure. A is correct (Guyton & Hall, p.180).

stem: Following an acute loss of 500 mL of plasma in a healthy adult, the plasma volume is restored to baseline within approximately:
reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Plasma proteins require about 3–4 days to recover, whereas red cell mass takes 4–8 weeks (Hemmings & Hopkins, p.818). Thus 8–12 hours is too short for complete plasma volume restitution.

options.E: BP in lower limb is normal

reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Lower-limb pressure is not reliably normal, and chronic baroreceptor resetting is not loss of baroreceptor function.

reason:
Explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Severe anaemia reduces arterial oxygen content despite a normal arterial PO2. Resting oxygen consumption is unchanged and increased cardiac output may not fully preserve delivery, so mixed venous oxygen content falls; heart rate increases. The original option A confuses increased fractional extraction with the absolute arterial–venous content difference, which by the Fick principle does not increase when cardiac output rises (West, p.227; Nunn & Lumb, p.344).

stem: In an otherwise healthy adult with intact sympathetic reflexes, which statement best describes the cardiovascular response to acute loss of 20% of blood volume?

options.A: A 20% loss produces irreversible shock in which cardiac output cannot return to normal
options.B: Arterial pressure decreases linearly once 20% has been lost
options.C: Systemic arterial pressure can be maintained at an adequate level until about 30–35% of blood volume has been lost
options.D: Cardiac output falls immediately and linearly from the onset of haemorrhage
options.E: Heart rate decreases as a sympathetic compensatory response

reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

With intact sympathetic reflexes, a 20% acute loss is compensated chiefly by vasoconstriction and tachycardia. Cardiac output falls before arterial pressure, while systemic arterial pressure can remain adequate up to about 30–35% loss (Hemmings & Hopkins, p.818; Guyton & Hall, p.282). Thus C is best; A, B, D and E contradict the reversible, nonlinear, tachycardic response.

stem: A low respiratory quotient in a septic patient is due to:

Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Respiratory quotient is VCO2/VO2 and is determined principally by metabolic substrate. Fat oxidation produces the lowest RQ, approximately 0.7, compared with 1.0 for carbohydrate. Lactic acid buffering and marked ventilation may increase measured respiratory exchange ratio rather than lower it (West’s Respiratory Physiology, p.236). Fever increases metabolic CO2 production, while ventilation and hypoxaemia do not specifically cause a low metabolic RQ.

Heat is not reliably the least effective: above the upper critical temperature, metabolic rate rises again (Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist, p.451). stem: In a resting patient at metabolic steady state, which of the following would predictably increase the cellular respiratory quotient by changing the predominant oxidised substrate?
reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Cellular RQ depends on oxidised substrate: carbohydrate has an RQ of 1.0, whereas fat is about 0.7. Low-lipid, high-carbohydrate TPN therefore increases steady-state RQ toward 1.0. Hyperventilation and acid-base CO2 washout principally alter pulmonary RER; strenuous exercise can make measured R exceed 1 (West, p.236), while cyanide decreases tissue oxygen uptake (West, p.229). The revised wording makes D uniquely correct.

reason: With fresh gas flowing, the inspiratory unidirectional valve is held shut during expiration, so continuing fresh gas cannot go forwards - it can only reach the compliant reservoir bag by travelling BACKWARDS along the rail and down through the absorbent. stem: The following airway pressure versus time curve is consistent with:
reason: Constant inspiratory flow against a fixed resistance produces an immediate resistive step at the start of inspiration and then a LINEAR rise in airway pressure as the lung fills - the ramp is the signature of volume control. stem: For two solutions separated by a semi-permeable membrane (Solution A: saline solution AND solution B: H2O): Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: A hydrostatic pressure applied to A will stop osmotic pressure
options.B: There will be bulk flow from A to B
options.C: The fluid level in B will go up
options.D: The NaCl concentration at A will remain the same

reason:
Source: Power & Kam, Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist, Ch. on body fluids (osmosis); Guyton & Hall, 14e, Ch. 4 (osmotic pressure)
Reasoning: A is hypertonic, so water moves B→A by osmosis. Osmotic pressure is defined as the hydrostatic pressure that must be applied to the concentrated solution (A) to just prevent this water movement. Hence B, C, D, E are all false (flow is B→A, level in A rises, [NaCl] in A falls).

stem: After ingestion of a meal:

Carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth via salivary α-amylase, while protein digestion begins in the stomach via pepsin (Guyton & Hall, pp. 780–782). Lingual lipase is secreted in the mouth but acts on swallowed triglyceride in the stomach; therefore, fat digestion does not begin in the mouth (pp. 782–783). stem: A drug is given at a dose of 50 mg/kg to a 70 kg man. The plasma concentration after giving it is 10 mg/ml. The elimination half-life is 8 hours. Clearance would be:
reason:
Reason modified by YMC on 5 Mar 2021
Reason modified by Hot Chocolate on 12 Feb 2021
Dose  = 50mg/kg x 70kg = 3500mg 
VD = Dose/Conc = 3500/10 = 350mL = 0.35L 

Cl = VD x k (where k is elimination rate constant) 
And t1/2 = ln2/k (so k = ln2/t1/2 = ln2/8 = 0.0866)

Therefore Cl = 0.35 x 0.0866 = 0.03L/hr 

Edit to previous poster:
- ln2 is 0.693 or 0.7 in an exam situation where you do not have a calculator
- So: Cl = (Vd x 0.7)/t1/2 = 0.03 L/h

stem: Nitrous oxide:

options.C: Is formed by heating oxygen & nitrogen
options.D: In tissues is slower to reabsorb than oxygen

reason:
Reason updated by acolyte on 24/2/2019.

- N2O supports combustion but is non-flammable
- N2O does not cause muscle relaxation alone (Nb. it potentiates the effects of musclerelaxants (but not as much as volatile agents)). At high concentrations, it can causemuscle rigidity
- N2O has a BGPC of 0.47, MWT of 44, a critical temperature of 36.5 °C, a boiling point of -88 °C
- N2O does not have a saturated vapour pressure at 20°C because it is a LIQUID at that temperature

- N2O has low blood:tissue partition coefficients (1.1, 1.2 and 2.3 for brain, muscle and fat, respectively), and would thus be absorbed faster into tissues due to large partial pressure gradients between blood and tissue

stem: Which inhalational agent is most likely to cause renal damage?
reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Methoxyflurane metabolism produces inorganic fluoride, including substantial intrarenal fluoride generation, causing collecting-tubule injury and vasopressin-resistant high-output renal insufficiency. Sevoflurane may form compound A, but typical human exposure has not caused clinically significant renal dysfunction. Desflurane and isoflurane are minimally metabolised. Therefore C is the single best answer (Evers, p.418; Stoelting, pp.153–154).

stem: Lignocaine works by:
reason:
- Main mechanism of action: Antagonism of VG-Na+ channels in excitable tissues
o Unionised LA diffuses across the phospholipid membrane into the more acidic axoplasm and then becomes ionized → Ionised LA binds to the inner portion of the channel (H- or internal-gate of α-subunit) from within the cell (but can also obstruct the channel physically at its external opening)
o LA binding to the channel is dependent on its conformational state → LAs have a high affinity for binding to the channel in its activated-open and inactivated- closed states:
 (i) LA gains access to its binding site within the channel ONLY it is in its activated open state during an AP
 (ii) LA then preferentially binds the channel during in inactivated-closed state and stabilises it in this conformation → Maintains channel in inactivated-closed state, and prevents reversion back to rested-closed state and activated-open state
o Antagonism of VG-Na+ channels results in ↓ Na+ permeability and flow across the membrane → This (i) slows the rate of rise in membrane depolarisation, and (ii) lowers the magnitude of membrane depolarisation → Produces two effects:
 VTHRESHOLD is met (Ie. lower [LA]) – AP is still generated but will have a slower impulse conduction (Ie. decreased slope of phase 0 of AP)
 VTHRESHOLD is not met (Ie. sufficient [LA]) – AP is not generated and impulse propagation is prevented (“conduction blockade”)
Note: The RMP and Level of VTHRESHOLD are NOT altered!
o LAs demonstrate “Frequency-dependent blockade”:
 A nerve that is repeatedly stimulated (Ie. ↑ frequency AP generated) is MORE sensitive to LA-induced conduction blockade than a nerve at rest
 This is because LA can only gain access to its binding site within the VG- Na+ channel to exert its effect when the channel is in an activated-open state during an AP
- Alternate mechanisms of action:
 Note: "Membrane expansion theory" is an alternate mechanism – Unionized lipid soluble LA dissolves into the phospholipid membrane and causes swelling of the lipoprotein matrix → Leads to disruption/inactivation of VG-Na+ channel
o (a) Antagonise other VG channels (VG-K+ channels and L-type Ca2+ channels), but with lower affinity than VG-Na+ channels
o (b) Also act on GPCRs

stem: Systemic toxicity of local anaesthetics:

options.D: rarely will CVS effects occur before CNS effects
options.E: symptomatic bradycardia will be followed by ventricular fibrillation

reason:
Reason updated by BB on 11/8/2019.

Could potentially be either D or E

Stoelting

The cardiovascular/central nervous system (CV/CNS) ratio describes the dose required to produce CV arrhythmias versus that required to produce seizures. If the ratio is lower, it implies a reduced safety margin for the local anesthetic compounds compared to the compound with higher ratio, to detect impending cardiotoxicity based on premonitory CNS signs.

The cardiovascular system is more resistant to the toxic effects of high plasma concentrations of local anesthetics than is the CNS.

Plasma concentrations of local anesthetics producing signs of central nervous system (CNS) toxicity depend on the specific drug involved. Lidocaine, mepivacaine, and prilocaine demonstrate effects on the CNS at plasma concentrations of 5 to 10 μg/mL. The typical plasma concentration of bupivacaine associated with seizures is 4.5 to 5.5 μg/mL.

Nevertheless, plasma lidocaine concentrations of 5 to 10 μg/mL, and equivalent plasma concentrations of other local anesthetics, may produce profound hypotension due to relaxation of arteriolar vascular smooth muscle and direct myocardial depression.

Excessive plasma concentrations of lidocaine may slow conduction of cardiac impulses through the heart, manifesting as prolongation of the P-R interval and QRS complex on the electrocardiogram. Effects of local anesthetics on calcium ion and potassium ion channels and local anesthetic-induced inhibition of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) production may also contribute to cardiac toxicity.

IV injection of bupivacaine or lidocaine to awake animals produces serious cardiac dysrhythmias only in animals receiving bupivacaine. Premature ventricular contractions, widening of the QRS complex, and ventricular tachycardia are the most common arrhythmias seen, though other arrhythmias including supraventricular tachycardia, atrioventricular heart block, and ST-T wave changes can also occur but are less common. Cardiotoxic plasma concentrations of bupivacaine are 8 to 10 μg/mL.

stem: What factor does not influence the peak plasma levels after epidural injection of local anaesthetic?

options.B: Natural vasoconstrictor activity of the drug

reason:
- Plasma [LA] achieved following injection of a LA is determined by its:
o (1) Rate of absorption from injection site into systemic circulation
 (a) Site of injection – Highly vascularised tissue → ↑ blood flow and ↑ systemic absorption 
IV > Trachea & mucosal membrane > Intercostal > Caudal > Paravertebral > Epidural > Brachial plexus > Sciatic > S/C > Intact skin
 (b) Use of vasoconstrictor agents (Eg. Adr) – Vasoconstriction → ↓ blood flow and ↓ systemic absorption
 (c) LA drug factors
 Dose applied – ↑ dose will lead to ↑ systemic absorption
 Intrinsic vasodilator activity – ↑ blood flow and ↑ systemic absorption
 Lipid solubility – ↑ lipid solubility → ↑ systemic absorption
 pKa of LA/Tissue pH – ↑ fraction unionised → ↑ systemic absorption
 Protein binding – LA highly-bound to tissue have ↓ systemic absorption
o (2)Rateoftissueredistribution
 (a) Tissue perfusion (C.O. and regional blood flows) – LA is the systemic circulation distributes first to highly perfused organs (lungs, brain, heart, liver, kidneys) → then to less well-perfused organs (incl muscle, fat, GIT)
 (b) Tissue/blood partition coefficient – Poor plasma-protein binding by LA and/or high lipid solubility of LA → ↑ redistribution to tissues; opposite is true
 (c) Tissue mass – Muscles are the largest reservoir for LA due to its high mass
o (3) Rate of clearance via metabolism and excretion
 LAs are cleared mainly by metabolism (ester LA via rapid hydrolysis by plasma and liver cholinesterases; amide LA via slow and complex hepatic metabolism by CYP450 MEOs)
 Since LAs are very poorly water-soluble → Minimal renal elimination of unchanged LA drug (< 5%)

stem: A solution of local anaesthetic contains 1:100,000 adrenaline. How much adrenaline has been added?
Regarding the addition of adrenaline to a local anaesthetic administered epidurally, which of the following is NOT true?

options.A: Significantly prolongs the duration of action of bupivacaine
options.B: Causes tissue acidosis at the site of injection

reason:
- Adrenaline (1:200,000 or 5 mcg/mL) causes localised tissue vasoconstriction results in reduced systemic absorption of the LA drug by 33% → Maintains LA drug levels at injection site → Produces following effects:
o (1) Increases the duration of LA activity at the injection site – Due to increased contact time of LA at injection site with nerve fibres
o (2) Increases the potency of LA (Ie. effect of LA achieved at a lower dose) → Has a sparing effect on LA dose given
o (3) Reduces risk of systemic LA toxicity – Reduces plasma [LA] 2° systemic absorption and lower dose needed to be delivered for effect
- HOWEVER, only select LA drugs (mainly lignocaine; but NOT bupivacaine, ropivacaine or levobupivacaine) have their effects prolonged by Adr – This is because more lipid soluble LAs are bound to surrounding soft tissues and are impacted less by effects of reduced tissue clearance 2° vasoconstriction
- Note that vasoconstriction 2° to adrenaline can cause tissue acidosis at the site of injection → ↓ fraction of unionised drug → ↓ speed of onset

stem: EMLA is a local anaesthetic solution that

options.B: Consists of a base and its respective local anaesthetics in an emulsion

reason:
Answer changed from D to B and reason modified by RM on 26 Feb 2023
Answer changed from B to D and reason modified by TLA on 18 Feb 2023
Reason edited by The Doc is Out on 12/7/2018

- Eutectic mixtures have 2 different substances that have the lowest melting point c.f. each individually, meaning that EMLA is an oil at room temperature, NOT that it is water soluble
- EMLA is an emulsion of lignocaine 2.5% & prilocaine 2.5% in a lipid base for a 5% total solution (with 80% concentration in the oil droplets in emulsion in a high water content vehicle)
- pH 8.5 with NaOH added to increase unionised fraction of each to about 60-70% (about 30-40% ionisation)
- causes vasoconstriction (whereas amethocaine / AnGel causes vasodilation)
- needs at least 45-60min to be effective (whereas amethocain / AnGel shouldn't be left >60min)

————————————————————————————————————————————————

Answer changed from B to D
- local anaesthetics are weak bases, thus EMLA must exist as a base with its respective acid in an emulsion (hence B incorrect)
 - pH of EMLA has been difficult to ascertain with most studies reporting high pH (9-9.4), including many reports of alkali burns. This pH would yield an ionised fraction 7.36% - 3.06%, ie. allows for a larger UN-ionised fraction which increases dermal absorption.
 - however if pH was 8.5 (as above), ionised fraction would be 20.08% (presuming pKa 7.9 for both lignocaine and prilocaine) -> therefore, C could be correct depending the examiner’s pH of EMLA (esp if someone can confirm this from a prescribed text…)
 - EMLA causes a BIPHASIC vasoactive reaction - “In healthy subjects, EMLA cream produced a biphasic vascular response with an initial vasoconstriction, maximal after 1.5 h of application. After prolonged application (greater than 3 h, vasodilatation occurred, presumably because of a smooth muscle relaxant effect of the analgesics.” (hence D correct - although time dependent, and clinically no-one ever wait 3h…so…could also argue incorrect)

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2532919/#:~:text=In%20healthy%20subjects%2C%20EMLA%20cream,relaxant%20effect%20of%20the%20analgesics.

reason:

stem: FE MD51 [Jul01] An intravenous infusion of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate to a healthy adult may cause:
reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Sodium bicarbonate generates CO2, which rapidly crosses cell membranes and may worsen intracellular acidosis (Hemmings & Hopkins, p.686; Stoelting, p.625). The 8.4% solution is hypertonic, and alkalosis decreases rather than increases ionized calcium. Respiratory alkalosis and rebound metabolic acidosis are not expected direct effects. The key is correct, although the claim that a healthy adult cannot develop acute metabolic alkalosis is overstated.

options.E: Bolus dose will increase systemic vascular resistance

reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Oxytocin is synthesized in hypothalamic magnocellular neurons and stored in the posterior pituitary (Kam & Power, p.396), so A is false. It has antidiuretic activity (Evers, p.954), excluding B. It is rapidly inactivated by peptidases, including oxytocinase, with hepatic metabolism, making C best. Bolus doses cause vascular smooth-muscle relaxation and reduced systemic vascular resistance (Stoelting, p.785); increased central venous pressure is not a consistent direct effect.

stem: Which drug is contraindicated in Pre eclampsia
reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Perindopril is an ACE inhibitor and is contraindicated during pregnancy because fetal renin–angiotensin system blockade can cause fetopathy, particularly fetal renal injury. Methyldopa, labetalol and hydralazine are established antihypertensive options in pregnancy. stem: Sulphonylureas:

options.B: Good in patients with depleted insulin stores
options.D: Increased glucose utilisation in the peripheries

reason:
- Sulphonylureas are derivatives of sulphonamides. There are several types:
o 1st generation (no longer used) – Chlorpropamide, Tolbutamide, Acetohexamide 
o 2nd generation (currently used) – Glibenclamide, Gliclazide, Glipizide
- Sulfonylureas work by stimulating insulin secretion from pancreatic islet (beta) cells (inhibits ATP-sensitive K+ channels, which results in depolarisation of beta-cells. This causes an influx of Ca2+ and stimulation of exocytosis of insulin storage granules) 
- Hence, they are not used for T1DM due to absence of beta cells (and insulin)
- Insulin released by sulfonylurea increases glucose transport into cells (hepatic and extrahepatic) due to increased translocation of GLUT 4 transporters to the membrane (BUT do not increase glucose utilisation!)
- Sulfonylureas are extensively protein-bound in plasma (esp albumin; 90-98%) due to it being weakly acidic – This results in a small VDISTRIBUTION
- Metformin (a biguanide) can cause a severe lactic acidosis – It binds to mitochondrial membranes and causes decreased IC ATP and increased IC AMP – This causes glucose to be metabolised anaerobically (rather than aerobically), leading to increased pyruvate production, which is then reduced to lactate

stem: Suxamethoniums mechanism of action

options.A: Inactivation of voltage gated sodium channels leading to prolonged depolarisation

reason:
Reason modified by anonymous on 15 Apr 2022
Answer changed from B to A anonymous on 14 Feb 2022
Answer changed from A to B anonymous on 3 Jul 2021
Answer and reason updated by DocKen on 6/12/2019.
Answer updated from "Open channel block" to "Inactivation of voltage gated sodium channels leading to prolonged depolarisation ".

Depolarization of the endplate by SCh results in opening of voltage gates in adjacent Na + channels, causing a wave of depolarization to sweep across the muscle, producing muscle contraction (fasciculation). Shortly after the voltage gates open, the inactivation gates close. Since the depolarizing SCh is not rapidly removed from the cleft, the endplate continues to be depolarized. As a result, the voltage gates of Na + channels adjacent to the endplate remain open and the inactivation gates stay closed and Na + cannot flow. Because the flow of ions through Na + channels in the perijunctional area is stopped, the perijunctional zone does not depolarize and the channels beyond the perijunctional zone are freed from the depolarizing influence. The perijunctional zone, in effect, acts as a buffer that shields the rest of the muscle from the events at the endplate. In other words, the muscle membrane is divided into three zones: the endplate, which is depolarized by SCh (or ACh); the perijunctional muscle membrane, in which the Na + channels exist in an inactivated state; and the rest of the muscle membrane, in which the Na + channels remain in the resting state.

Open channel block refers to a channel that is opened and then blocked e.g. MoA of local anaesthetics

Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

For nondepolarizing blockers, onset is inversely related to potency: low potency permits a larger molar dose and concentration gradient, accelerating delivery to the neuromuscular junction (Stoelting, p.345; Evers, p.632). Organ-independent elimination affects recovery and predictability, not onset. The key is correct, but the placeholder options required repair.

stem: Which statement about atracurium is correct?

options.A: Its metabolites have clinically significant neuromuscular blocking activity.
options.B: Its metabolism is impaired by pseudocholinesterase deficiency.
options.C: Its Hofmann elimination is affected only by temperature.
options.D: It undergoes ester hydrolysis catalysed by an esterase system unrelated to plasma cholinesterase.
options.E: Its elimination depends primarily on hepatic and renal function.

reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Atracurium undergoes ester hydrolysis to a quaternary acid and alcohol via an esterase system unrelated to plasma cholinesterase (Foundations of Anesthesia, p.433). It also undergoes temperature- and pH-dependent Hofmann elimination, so C is false. Its metabolites are inactive at the neuromuscular junction, pseudocholinesterase deficiency does not impair its metabolism, and elimination is not primarily hepatic or renal (Evers, p.635).

options.B: It is eliminated primarily by hepatic and secondarily by renal mechanisms.
options.C: It undergoes significant metabolism before excretion.

reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Rocuronium is eliminated mainly by hepatobiliary excretion and to a lesser extent by renal excretion, without significant metabolism. Foundations of Anesthesia, p.432, explicitly describes its elimination as primarily hepatic and secondarily renal; Evers, p.657, quantifies biliary excretion as >75% and renal excretion as 10–25%.

"Sinus bradycardia, junctional rhythm, and even sinus arrest may follow administration of succinylcholine. These
cardiac effects reflect the actions of succinylcholine at cardiac muscarinic cholinergic receptors where the drug
mimics the physiologic effects of acetylcholine.

stem: Which of the following generally does NOT prolong nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade?
reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Volatile anaesthetics, aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, hypothermia, and magnesium sulfate potentiate nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade and prolong its duration or recovery (Stoelting, pp.345, 355). Hyperthermia is therefore the exception. The existing explanation’s claim of uniformly increased metabolism and excretion is insufficiently supported and may be drug-dependent.

stem: The dibucaine number for a normal person is:
reason:
- “Dibucaine number” (DN) is the % inhibition of normal PC activity in metabolising benzylcholine substrate in the presence of 10-5 mol/L dibucaine (an amide LA)
- DN is proportional to the level of PC function in hydrolysing SCh – DN80 means normal PC, while DN20 means homozygous atypical PC variant, and DN40-60 means heterozygous atypical PC variant
- Note – DN does NOT reflect the quantity of enzyme in plasma (only its quality), thus reduced PC levels (Ie. liver disease) will have a DN80 but prolonged SCh duration of action

stem: Which drug inhibits acetylcholinesterase by reversible electrostatic binding that denies acetylcholine access, without carbamylating the enzyme?
reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Edrophonium binds reversibly by electrostatic interaction at the anionic region of acetylcholinesterase and denies acetylcholine access. Neostigmine, pyridostigmine and physostigmine instead carbamylate the catalytic serine, producing slowly reversible enzyme inactivation. Thus D is the single best answer for competitive inhibition; E is correct only if the question merely asks which drugs inhibit acetylcholinesterase (Rang & Dale, pp.198–199; Foundations, p.438).

stem: In reversing neuromuscular blockade, which of the following combinations is best matched with respect to time of onset?
reason:
- Reversal drug needs to be given concurrently with an anticholinergic drug to minimise the unwanted muscarinic ACh effects of AChEi. It is ideal to give an anticholinergic drug with a faster onset than AChEi to minimise its muscarinic effects (esp CVS effects, such as bradycardia)
o Edrophonium – Given with atropine as both have rapid onset. Glycopyrrolate should NOT be given due to risk of bradycardia unless it is administered minutes prior to edrophonium
o Neostigmine – Can be given with either atropine or glycopyrrolate as neostigmine has an intermediate onset of 3-5 mins. Atropine is less favoured due to its faster onset (causes an initial tachycardia which is an issue in patients with CVD) and CNS side-effects
o Pyridostigmine – Can be given with either atropine or glycopyrrolate due to its very slow onset. Both will give initial tachycardia, but glycopyrrolate is preferred due to slower onset

stem: Regarding anticholinesterase agents, which statement is correct?

options.A: The duration of action of carbamates is determined by the time required for dissociation from the anionic site.
options.B: Carbamates inhibit acetylcholinesterase by acetylating the serine hydroxyl at the esteratic site.
options.C: Carbamates transfer a carbamyl group to the serine hydroxyl at the esteratic site, and recovery is prolonged because the carbamylated enzyme hydrolyses slowly.
options.D: Edrophonium inhibits acetylcholinesterase by phosphorylating the esteratic site.
options.E: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase solely by readily reversible ionic binding to the anionic site.

reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

C is correct. Carbamates transfer a carbamyl group to the serine hydroxyl at the esteratic site. The carbamylated enzyme hydrolyses slowly, so recovery takes minutes rather than microseconds (Rang & Dale, p.199). This is not acetylation or dissociation from the anionic site.

stem: Carbamylation of acetylcholinesterase: (Jul02: Phosphorylation of acetylcholinesterase: )
reason:
- AChEi such as Pyridostigmine, Physostigmine, Neostigmine act via reversible inhibition by forming a carbamylated enzyme complex with AChE through covalent bonds
o Anionic site is bound by quaternary ammonium group of the AChEi via an electrostatic bond, but the esteratic site hydrolyses the AChEi’s ester linkage and results in the transfer of a carbamate group to the esteratic site
o Carbamylated AChE is inactive and cannot bind/hydrolyze ACh until the carbamate-ACh bond at the esteratic site dissociates slowly via hydrolysis (t 1⁄2 ~ 15-30 mins)

stem: Release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate:

options.B: Only in response to action potential

reason:
- Gentamicin attenuates presynaptic ACh release by stabilising the prejunctional membrane (by competing with Ca2+)
- Botox attenuates presynaptic ACh release by cleaving enzymes that facilitate presynaptic release of ACh from vesicles
- Hemicholinium inhibits ACh synthesis (by blocking choline transport into the nerve)
- Release of presynaptic ACh can occur:
o (i) In absence of a motor nerve impulse – Random release of a single “quanta” of ACh into the synapse independent of nerve terminal depolarisation. This produces a “Miniature EPP” (MEPP) of < 1 mV only, which is insufficient to activate perijunctional VG-Na+ channels and trigger a muscle AP
o (ii) In response to a motor nerve impulse – A single nerve AP increases the nerve terminal MP from -90 mV at rest to VTHRESHOLD of -45 mV causing it to depolarise. This activates nerve terminal Adenylyl cyclase to produce cAMP, which triggers opening of Ca2+ channels and an influx of Ca2+. The rise in IC [Ca2+] causes vesicles to fuse with the membrane and exocytose ACh into the synaptic cleft. A single nerve impulse will release > 200 quanta of ACh, which is sufficient to generate a summated motor end plate potential and trigger a muscle AP
Nb. 1 quanta of ACh = 100-200 synaptic vesicles = 5000-10,000 ACh molecules

stem: Which process is principally responsible for the medium duration of acetylcholinesterase inhibition by neostigmine?

options.A: Covalent carbamylation of the serine hydroxyl group at the esteratic (catalytic) site
options.B: Electrostatic binding only to the esteratic site
options.C: Reversible ionic binding only to the anionic site
options.D: Formation of a carbamylated enzyme that is hydrolysed more rapidly than acetylated acetylcholinesterase
options.E: Irreversible phosphorylation of the serine hydroxyl group at the esteratic site

reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

Neostigmine first binds through its positively charged nitrogen to the anionic site, then transfers its carbamyl group covalently to the serine hydroxyl at the esteratic site. Slow hydrolysis of this carbamylated enzyme over minutes prolongs inhibition. Thus repaired option A is best. Originally, C was also true and E was a placeholder (Rang & Dale, p.199; Foundations of Anesthesia, p.438).

stem: Regarding anticholinesterases:

options.B: Quaternary ammonium anticholinesterases have a larger volume of distribution than non- depolarising muscle relaxants
options.C: Edrophonium has a slower onset of action than neostigmine
options.D: Neostigmine has a longer duration of action than pyridostigmine
options.E: Edrophonium binds covalently to the esteratic site of acetylcholine

reason:
- AChEi with quaternary ammonium group (edrophonium, neostigmine, pyridostigmine) are poorly lipid soluble and do not cross cell membrane barriers (Eg. BBB, GIT, placenta); Tertiary amines (physostigmine and OP-type AChEi) are lipid soluble and can cross cell membranes easily
- AChEi generally have a large Vd (0.7-1.4 L/kg) due to extensive tissue storage in organs (esp liver and kidneys), as compared to ND NMBA
- Edrophonium has the most rapid onset (1-2 min) due to its presynaptic effects, while neostigmine (3-5 mins), physostigmine (5 mins) and pyridostigmine (10-15 mins) have more delayed onset due to their postsynaptic mechanism of action
- At clinical doses, they are similar between agents (except for OP’s which act indefinitely) – Edrophonium and Neostigmine 40-60 mins (although Edrophonium is traditionally a short-acting agent (10 mins) at small non-clinical doses); Physostigmine 1-2 hrs; Pyridostigmine > 2 hrs; OPs indefinite
- Edrophonium acts via reversible inhibition of AChE by forming a drug-enzyme complex through non-covalent bonds – Anionic site is bound by quaternary ammonium group of the AChEi via an electrostatic bond, while the esteratic site is bound by a hydroxyl group of the AChEi via a hydrogen bond
- Topical AChEi (ecothiopate) is used to treat glaucoma (NOT oral!)

stem: Following reversal of a nondepolarizing neuromuscular block, which finding at the adductor pollicis is the best indicator of adequate neuromuscular recovery?

options.B: No visually or tactually detectable fade with double-burst stimulation
options.C: No visually or tactually detectable fade during 200-Hz tetanic stimulation

reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

stem: The earliest, most sensitive marker for opioid induced ventilatory impairment is:
reason:

stem: One mg of alfentanil is administered to a pregnant woman at term for induction of anaesthesia prior to a caesarean section. What percentage of unionised drug (of alfentanil) will be present in the fetal blood?
reason:
Answer changed from B to D by anonymous on 16 Jul 2025
Answer changed from D to B and reason modified by LD on 26 May 2024
I couldn't find a single textbook reference to this scenario but from first principles; the pKa of alfentanil is 6.5. Using a pH of 7.25 (foetal pH) and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, this gives us a value of 85% unionised. The closest answer is therefore D.
Dr mitta 06:56, 3 December 2015 (CST)

--85% is the percentage of unionised drug, but I reckon the question is about " What percentage of unionised drug (of alfentanil) will be present in the fetal blood" as from single bolus dose, 10% pulmonary first pass metabolism, then 85% of the rest 90% is about 77%. On the other hand, percentage of uterus blood perfusion is almost 600ml/6000ml-->10% so 10% of 77% will cross placenta which is 7.7% almost 10% then B is correct.if 90% crosses placenta then we administer opioid to baby instead of mother!
Please comment where I am wrong?
F/M ratio, MTF = 0.22. With 89% unionised at pH 7.4 (Chestnut's Obstetric Anaesthesia, 5th ed, table 4-3.) If question is asking for how much of the drug is unionised in fetal blood - 85-90% (see above) If question is asking for how much drug is present in fetal circulation unionised as a fraction of total maternal + fetal drug, then it is ~20% --Drjd 22:35, 19 May 2016 (CDT)

Alfentanil is 90% unionised in maternal plasma, but 90% of this is bound to AAG, which decreases its degree of placental transfer, leaving only 10% of the unionised drug to transfer across to the foetus. The foetal blood is more acidic and so there will be a lesser degree of ionisation but overall still closer to 10%. 90% does not make sense otherwise we would just be administering the drug to the foetus.

reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

reasoning: ~50% of filtered urea is passively reabsorbed in the PCT (driven by Na+/water reabsorption raising luminal [urea]). Further variable reabsorption occurs in the inner medullary collecting duct (ADH-dependent), but of the options the PCT is the principal reabsorptive site.

stem: Which ONE of the following is not involved in the regulation of glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (autoregulation)
reasoning: GFR is autoregulated over MAP ~75-170 mmHg, so arterial pressure within range does not regulate it. JGA (TGF), distal tubule Na (macula densa sensing), and afferent/efferent tone all regulate GFR.
note: some argue D (distal Na) is the intended answer if one rejects the MD-TGF link; B is the accepted key.

stem: With regard to glomerular filtration:

options.B: Efferent - afferent hydrostatic pressure is driving force
options.C: Is equal for cationic & anionic molecules
options.D: All cross if < 8 nm in diameter
options.E: Occurs only when perfusion pressure exceeds 100 mmHg

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (autoregulation & filtration barrier)
reasoning: Autoregulation (afferent arteriolar tone) keeps RBF/GFR constant. The driving force is glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (not "efferent-afferent"); the barrier is charge-selective (cations filter more readily than anions) and size-selective (freely filters <~4 nm, excludes >~8 nm - so "all <8 nm" is wrong). Filtration occurs across the whole autoregulatory range, not only >100 mmHg.
reconstructed: option E (plausible distractor)

stem: Significant tubular reabsorption occurs with:
reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e; Kam & Power
reasoning: Phosphate is significantly reabsorbed (~85-90%). Creatinine is filtered and (net) secreted, not significantly reabsorbed. Urea reabsorption is variable/partial (40-60%). Sulphate reabsorption is limited. Phosphate is the best single answer for "significant reabsorption."

stem: Increased GFR is caused by

options.D: Increased chloride delivery to the macula densa

reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Increased cardiac output may raise glomerular capillary pressure and increase GFR (Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.431). Afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and efferent arteriolar vasodilatation reduce glomerular capillary pressure, while increased chloride delivery to the macula densa activates tubuloglomerular feedback that lowers GFR. The original key incorrectly assumes an unstated restriction to complete autoregulation.

stem: The formula for GFR is:
reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e, p 27: NFP = (PGC - PBC) - (πGC - πBC)
reasoning: Expanding the net filtration pressure, GFR = Kf[(HPG - HPB) - (OPG - OPB)] = Kf(HPG - HPB - OPG + OPB). Glomerular oncotic pressure (OPG) OPPOSES filtration (subtracted); Bowman's oncotic pressure (OPB) FAVOURS filtration (added). Option E incorrectly subtracts OPB.
note: heavily flip-flopped in the recall (B vs E). B is correct once the brackets are expanded; texts often write it as (HPG-HPB)-(πGC) because πBC≈0.

stem: Using average daily values of 180 L of water filtered and 179 L reabsorbed, what percentage of filtered water is reabsorbed by the kidneys?
reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Using the stated average values, fractional water reabsorption is 179/180 × 100 = 99.4%. Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.433, lists 180 L/day filtered, 179 L/day reabsorbed, and 99.4% reabsorbed. Thus D, rather than C, is the best answer.

stem: Water excretion by the kidney is due to:

options.C: Passive secretion in the collecting tubules

reason:
Source: Kam & Power, p 231; Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e
reasoning: Tubular water movement follows osmotic gradients created by solute (mainly Na+) reabsorption - i.e., osmosis. Water is not actively transported; facilitated diffusion via aquaporins is a component but osmosis (the osmotic driving force) is the most complete single answer.

stem: Glomerulotubular balance:

options.D: Ability to increase tubular absorption in response to an increase in filtered load

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (glomerulotubular balance); Kam & Power
reasoning: Glomerulotubular balance is the intrinsic ability of the PCT to reabsorb a constant FRACTION (~65%) of the filtered load, so absolute reabsorption rises when filtered load rises. It is distinct from tubuloglomerular feedback (which involves the JGA/arterioles).

stem: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR):

options.A: Is independent of the size of the capillary bed
options.B: Depends only on the hydrostatic and osmotic pressure differences across the capillary
options.C: Is determined by the same forces governing filtration across all other capillaries
options.D: Depends only on the permeability of the capillary

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (Starling forces); Kam & Power
reasoning: GFR = Kf x NFP, governed by the same Starling forces as other capillaries. It DOES depend on capillary bed size (Kf includes surface area), on both pressures AND permeability (so "only" statements are wrong), and it is passive ultrafiltration (no active transport).

stem: Increase in GFR occurs with
reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (Starling forces)
reasoning: Hypoproteinaemia lowers glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (πGC) → raises NFP → raises GFR. SNS stimulation and decreased RBF lower GFR; ureteric obstruction raises Bowman's hydrostatic pressure → lowers GFR.

stem: Regarding urea:

options.C: Transcortical gradient is responsible for creating a concentrated urine
options.D: Tubular reabsorption is variable and depends on the state of hydration
options.E: It is actively secreted in the proximal tubule

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (urea recycling); Kam & Power (urea cycle)
reasoning: Urea is formed in the liver from arginine (→ ornithine via arginase), not "from ornithine" (A imprecise). ~40-60% (not 10%) is reabsorbed. The correct term is the cortico-medullary (not "transcortical") gradient. Urea reabsorption is variable and ADH/hydration-dependent (D correct). Urea is passively handled, not actively secreted in the PCT.
original: D (recall listed D and E as "?")
reconstructed: options D (the correct hydration-dependent statement) and E (plausible distractor). Note: original A-C are all flawed - likely a poorly-remembered question.

stem: Regarding water reabsorption in the collecting tubules:

options.B: collecting tubules able to reabsorb 60-70% of water
options.D: loops of Henle are ONLY located in the renal medulla

reason:
Source: Kam & Power, pp 258-261; Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e
reasoning: Of the offered options, C is the "least wrong": renin (via AII → ADH release) indirectly influences collecting-duct water reabsorption. Aldosterone controls Na+/K+, not water (A wrong); the CD reabsorbs only ~5-20% of water, most is PCT (B wrong); LoH of cortical nephrons extend into the cortex (D wrong); water reabsorption in the CD is critically ADH-dependent (E wrong).
note: weak/poorly-remembered question - C selected as best available; the true determinant is ADH.
reconstructed: option E (plausible distractor)

stem: Regarding the Loop of Henle:

options.A: active transport of Na+ into tubules
options.B: active transport of Cl- out of tubules
options.C: active transport of K+ into tubules

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e; Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (NKCC2 in TAL)
reasoning: The TAL reabsorbs Na+, K+, Cl- OUT of the lumen (2° active transport) - so Cl- out (B) is correct. Ions are not pumped INTO the lumen; the ascending limb is water-impermeable; renin is made in the JGA (afferent arteriole), not the LoH.

stem: Water handling by the kidney: if 180 L of water is filtered per day and 179 L is reabsorbed, what percentage of filtered water is reabsorbed?
reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Water reabsorption is 179/180 × 100 = 99.4%. Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.433, lists 180 L/day filtered, 179 L/day reabsorbed, and 1 L/day excreted. The original 99% key reflects a different set of average values; specifying the volumes removes this source-dependent ambiguity.

stem: Which of the following decrease secretion of potassium in the distal convoluted tubule
reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (K+ secretion); Guyton & Hall, 14th ed
reasoning: Acute acidosis reduces K+ secretion (ENaC/ROMK down-regulated → less K+ into lumen). Aldosterone and vasopressin increase K+ secretion; a saline load (increased distal flow/Na delivery) increases secretion; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors increase distal Na delivery/flow → increase K+ secretion.

stem: The juxtaglomerular apparatus (repeat)

options.A: Macula densa is located in the PROXIMAL ascending loop
options.B: Granular cells are in the wall of the afferent arteriole
options.C: Mesangial cells are inside Bowman's capsule

reason:
Source: Kam & Power, Ch 7, p 224; Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e

The macula densa is at the DISTAL end of the thick ascending limb (A wrong; and it does not secrete renin, D wrong). Extraglomerular mesangial cells lie OUTSIDE Bowman's capsule (C wrong). Podocytes cover glomerular capillaries, not the afferent arteriole (E wrong).

options.A: Has both sympathetic and parasympathetic supply
options.B: Contains renin-secreting granular cells in the efferent arteriole
options.C: Mesangial cells lie within Bowman's capsule
options.D: Juxtaglomerular cells lie in the afferent arterioles
options.E: Macula densa cells are in the thick ascending loop of Henle

reason:
Source: Kam & Power, Ch 7, p 224
reasoning: JG (granular) cells lie in the AFFERENT arteriole wall (D correct). The macula densa IS in the (distal) thick ascending limb, so E is also correct - a genuine two-answer item. The JGA has sympathetic (not parasympathetic) supply; granular cells are in the afferent (not efferent) arteriole; extraglomerular mesangial cells lie outside Bowman's capsule.

stem: The regulation of GFR is not influenced by
reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (autoregulation)
reasoning: GFR is autoregulated across MAP ~75-170 mmHg, so MAP within range does not influence it. JGA, macula densa (TGF) and afferent/efferent arteriolar tone all regulate GFR.

stem: Renal water reabsorption occurs predominantly by
reason:
Source: Kam & Power, p 231
reasoning: Water reabsorption is driven by osmosis - solute (Na+) reabsorption lowers luminal osmolality and water follows. Water is never actively transported.

stem: Glomerulotubular balance refers to:

options.A: The maintenance of the proportion reabsorbed to filtered load.
options.B: The matching of urine output to GFR
options.C: The regulation of GFR by the macula densa
options.D: Urine output maintained constant in the face of changing GFR
options.E: Urine output:GFR ratio maintained despite changes in RPP

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e; Kam & Power
reasoning: Glomerulotubular balance = proximal tubular reabsorption changes in parallel with filtered load so that a constant PROPORTION (~two-thirds) is reabsorbed despite GFR changes. Option C describes tubuloglomerular feedback, not glomerulotubular balance.

stem: Urea

options.A: can be used to measure intracellular space by the dilution principle
options.B: responsible for 80% of renal medullary osmolality of 1400mOsm/kg
options.C: synthesised in the liver from ammonia
options.D: formation via urea cycle produces 3ATP/molecule of urea synthesised
options.E: reabsorption by the nephron is 20% of the filtered load

reason:
Source: Kam & Power (urea cycle); Ganong (medullary osmolality); Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e
reasoning: Urea is synthesised in the liver from ammonia (deamination of amino acids). It contributes ~46% (~650 mOsm/kg), not 80%, of medullary osmolality; the urea cycle CONSUMES ~3 ATP (does not produce); nephron reabsorption is ~40-60% (not 20%); urea distributes in total body water, not just ICF (A wrong).

stem: Regarding the loop of Henle in the kidney:

options.A: Water is actively transported out of the descending limb
options.B: Chloride is actively reabsorbed in the ascending loop of Henle
options.C: The descending limb is impermeable to water
options.D: Sodium is actively pumped into the lumen of the ascending limb
options.E: Tubular fluid is hypotonic to plasma at the top of the ascending limb

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e ("ascending limb = diluting segment")
reasoning: The TAL reabsorbs more solute than water, so fluid leaving the loop into the DCT is hypo-osmotic to plasma (E correct). B is also true (Cl- is actively/2° actively reabsorbed in the TAL) - options likely imperfectly recalled. Water is never actively transported; the descending limb is highly water-permeable; Na is pumped OUT of (not into) the ascending limb lumen.
note: B is also correct; E is the recall key (secondary active transport debated as "active").
reconstructed: options A, C and D (plausible distractors)

stem: Which of the following constricts both the afferent AND the efferent glomerular arterioles?
reason:
Source: Kam & Power, Ch 41, p 250 ("Angiotensin II constricts afferent and efferent arterioles")
reasoning: AII constricts BOTH arterioles (efferent > afferent at physiological levels). ANP dilates the afferent; dopamine is a renal vasodilator; aldosterone acts on distal tubular Na/K, not arteriolar calibre.
note: official ANZCA remembered question.

stem: The plasma in the vasa recta leaving the renal medulla when compared to that entering the medulla has

options.A: osmolarity that is greater but the volume is reduced
options.B: osmolarity that is the same but the volume is greater
options.C: osmolarity that is reduced but the volume is greater
options.D: osmolarity and volume vary depending on the presence of ADH

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e ("volume of blood leaving the vessels is higher than entering, osmolarity close to plasma")
reasoning: Countercurrent exchange in the vasa recta means blood leaving the medulla has near-plasma osmolarity (little net change) but greater volume (net water pick-up from the interstitium), preserving the medullary gradient.
note: official ANZCA remembered question.

stem: In an average healthy adult, glomerular water filtration by the kidneys:

options.C: Has no more than 90% of the filtered water reabsorbed
options.D: Freely filters most drugs because their molecular weight is less than 600
options.E: Is approximately 20% of renal blood flow

reason:
Explanation supplied in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — the key is the Black Bank's and is not examiner-verified.

GFR in an average adult is approximately 125 mL/min, equivalent to 180 L/day. About 20% of renal plasma flow, not renal blood flow, is filtered (Guyton & Hall, p.317). The original option E was therefore also true, making the unmodified question ambiguous; the repaired option E leaves B as the single best answer.

stem: Kidney:

options.E: Cannot produce urine hypotonic to plasma

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e, p 100; Brandis, The Physiology Viva
reasoning: Max urine concentration is ~1200-1400 mOsm/kg; A (1200) is the classic figure. Min is ~40-100 mOsm/kg, so B (100) is also defensible. Urine CAN be hypotonic to plasma (E wrong); max is not 300 (D wrong); min ~20 (C) is too low.
note: A and B are both defensible; A is the recall key. Some texts quote max 1400, making no option exact (inter-text difference, not an error).
reconstructed: options D and E (plausible distractors)

stem: Angiotensin II causes:

options.A: Increases proximal tubular reabsorption of Na & H2O & increases secretion of K+
options.B: Increases distal tubular reabsorption of Na & H2O & decreases secretion of K+
options.C: Decreases distal tubular reabsorption of Na & H2O

reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Angiotensin II directly increases proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption and stimulates aldosterone secretion; aldosterone increases distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. It also reduces renal blood flow and sodium and water excretion. Thus A is the single best answer (Guyton & Hall, pp. 344–345; Kam & Power, pp. 283–284).

stem: Pressure diuresis:

options.A: Due to decreased reabsorption of Na+ & water in peritubular capillaries

reason:
Source: Kam & Power, 4th ed, p 250; Guyton & Hall, 14th ed (pressure natriuresis/diuresis)
reasoning: A rise in arterial/renal pressure raises peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure and washes out the medullary gradient → decreased Na+/water reabsorption → increased excretion. Pressure diuresis is NOT driven by the macula densa/JGA, and it is associated with DECREASED ADH/AII, not increased.

stem: What is the minimum amount of urine required to excrete 600mOsm
reason:
Source: Kam & Power (obligatory urine volume); Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e
reasoning: 600 mOsm ÷ maximum urine concentration (~1200-1400 mOsm/kg) ≈ 430-500 mL - the obligatory urine loss. 500 mL is the closest option.

stem: Biggest contribution to urine concentration by:

options.A: Na+ absorption in thick ascending limb
options.B: Passive diffusion of urea in collecting ducts
options.C: Chloride absorption in distal convoluted tubule
options.D: Water reabsorption in the descending limb of the loop of Henle
options.E: Potassium secretion in the collecting duct

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (urea recycling); Kam & Power
reasoning: Passive urea reabsorption from the inner medullary collecting duct (ADH-dependent) contributes roughly half of medullary interstitial osmolality (~650 mOsm/kg) - the biggest single contributor offered here. TAL NaCl reabsorption is the other major contributor but urea is the emphasised answer.
reconstructed: options D and E (plausible distractors)
note: A (TAL Na reabsorption) is also a major contributor; B is the recall key.

stem: A healthy adult excretes approximately 600 mOsm of solute per day and can achieve a maximal urine osmolality of approximately 1200 mOsm/kg H₂O. What is the approximate minimum obligatory urine volume?
reason:
Black Bank key corrected, and explained, in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

A usual daily solute load of 600 mOsm and maximal urine concentration of 1200 mOsm/L give 600/1200 = 0.5 L/day, the obligatory urine volume (Guyton & Hall, pp.352–353). Kam & Power p.270 gives 430 mL using 1400 mOsm/kg H2O, so 500 mL/day remains the best approximate option. A–D describe non-urinary losses and do not answer the stem.

stem: Mechanism of action of ADH:

options.A: Insertion of water channels (pores) into basolateral membrane
options.C: Insertion of water channels into luminal (apical) membrane
options.E: Removal of water pores from apical membrane

reason:
Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (AQP2); Kam & Power
reasoning: ADH (V2 → cAMP) inserts AQP2 water channels into the APICAL (luminal) membrane of collecting duct principal cells. Water then exits via AQP3/4 basolaterally. ADH actually reduces GFR (afferent constriction) and does not primarily act by DCT Na uptake.

stem: In a patient with significant hypovolaemia and increased osmolality:

options.A: Decreased sodium reabsorption at distal tubule & collecting duct
options.B: Increased water reabsorption at proximal tubule
options.C: Increased water reabsorption at ascending loop of Henle
options.D: Increased water permeability of collecting duct

Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (ADH action)
reasoning: Hypovolaemia + raised osmolality → maximal ADH → increased AQP2-mediated water permeability of the collecting duct (D). Distal Na reabsorption INCREASES (aldosterone); PCT water reabsorption is constant/obligatory; the ascending limb is water-impermeable regardless of ADH.

stem: The minimum pH that the urine can create is

Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 8e, p 159 ("minimum urinary pH ~4.4")

Source: Vander's Renal Physiology, 9e (PCT reabsorbs ~65% under all conditions)

stem: ADH secretion affect:

stem: In order to excrete an osmotic load of 600mOsm/day, the minimum daily urine output is:

Source: Kam & Power, 2nd ed, p 221

stem: Role of ADH:

options.A: Inserts aquaporin channels into basolateral membrane of collecting ducts
options.D: Stimulates renin release from granular cells

Source: Kam & Power, pp 240, 330-1

stem: In regards to the effect of ANP on the kidney:

stem: In a drug eliminated by zero-order kinetics, which of the following is true?

Clearance and half-time are distinct quantities with different units. This is consistent with the constant-rate description of zero-order kinetics in Rang & Dale, p.151, and Hemmings & Hopkins, p.113.

stem: Main mechanism for use of adrenaline in cardiac arrest to achieve ROSC
reason:
Transcribed from a '2025 MCQ' Anki recall deck (taken to be the 2025.1 / P25A sitting: it shares almost nothing with the 2025.2 recall already in the corpus). Recall only — the answer, where present, is the deck author's and is unverified.

Deck note: In a cardiac arrest (where there is no effective cardiac output), the goal of adrenaline is not to make the heart beat faster or stronger—because the heart is often not beating in a coordinated way at all. Instead, the primary goal is to increase Coronary Perfusion Pressure (CPP). Alpha-1 Mediated Vasoconstriction: Adrenaline causes profound peripheral vasoconstriction (increasing Systemic Vascular Resistance). Blood Shunting: This constricts the peripheral vasculature, shunting blood away from the "non-critical" periphery (skin, muscle, gut) back toward the central circulation. Increased Diastolic Pressure: By increasing the resistance in the systemic circuit, the aortic diastolic pressure rises during the "recoil" phase of chest compressions. Coronary Perfusion: Since the heart is perfused during diastole, this higher aortic pressure pushes blood into the coronary arteries, providing the myocardium with the oxygen it needs to potentially restart a coordinated rhythm (ROSC)

Deck note: 2-4mmHg In a young, healthy adult, the normal gradient between PaCO2 (arterial carbon dioxide) and ETCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) is typically between 2 to 4 mmHg. This is the difference in CO₂ concentrations between the arterial blood and the exhaled air. PaCO2 is the amount of CO₂ in arterial blood, which reflects the respiratory function and metabolic CO₂ production. ETCO2 is the amount of CO₂ present at the end of exhalation, which is influenced by the alveolar ventilation and how efficiently CO₂ is being expelled. The gradient exists because there is usually a small difference between the CO₂ levels in the alveoli (where gas exchange occurs) and the arterial blood, mainly due to ventilation-perfusion mismatches or physiological dead space

This increases insulin levels and can cause hypoglycemia, particularly if the drug is taken without sufficient food intake or in cases of renal impairment. Sulfonylureas are known to have a high risk of causing hypoglycemia, especially when the dose is not adjusted appropriately. However, if used in combination with other insulin secretagogues, there may be an increased risk. Acarbose (D): Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor that slows the breakdown of carbohydrates in the intestine, which leads to a slower absorption of glucose. It does not typically cause hypoglycemia on its own, but in combination with other drugs that increase insulin secretion, it can contribute to hypoglycemia

Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

The bicarbonate system cannot buffer carbonic acid because carbonic acid is its own acid component. Respiratory acidosis is therefore buffered by non-bicarbonate buffers, principally haemoglobin, with contributions from intracellular and plasma proteins. Kam & Power, p.308, states that more than 90% of blood buffering of carbonic acid is contributed by haemoglobin.

stem: How long does it take for the effects of omeprazole to reverse and gastric acid secretion to return to normal?
reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+-ATPase. Acid secretion returns only after new proton pumps are generated, which takes several days despite omeprazole’s plasma half-life of 0.5–1 hour (Evers, p.846).

stem: ABO incompatibility reaction from PRBCs results from:
reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

ABO-incompatible packed donor red cells carry A or B antigens that react with the recipient’s pre-existing anti-A or anti-B antibodies, predominantly IgM, causing agglutination, complement activation and intravascular haemolysis. Donor plasma antibody is minimal in packed red cells and is diluted in the recipient. Kam & Power, pp. 329, 348, 351.

stem: Which of these prevent against microshock?
reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Equipotential earthing connects surrounding metalwork so that it remains at the same potential, preventing small potential differences from driving current through a patient, including via an intracardiac conductor. A fuse protects against large fault currents; an RCD typically trips at about 30 mA, far above microshock levels; and a line isolation monitor detects rather than interrupts the first earth fault. Essentials of Anaesthetic Equipment, pp.263–264.

stem: Graph of slow action potential. What happens with increased SNS activity?
reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Sympathetic stimulation increases cAMP and enhances the funny current and calcium-channel activity in nodal pacemaker cells, increasing the slope of phase 4 depolarization and therefore the firing rate. It also speeds, rather than decreases, AV nodal conduction. Kam & Power, pp. 170–173.

stem: In Marsh TCI, what is the difference between a 20 year old vs 80 year old who weigh 70kg?

options.C: Unchanged infusion rate and bolus dose
options.D: Altered infusion rate AND bolus dose

reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

The standard Marsh propofol model scales compartment volumes and clearances by body weight but does not include age as a covariate. Thus, for two 70 kg patients given the same target, it calculates the same loading bolus and infusion profile. Actual propofol requirements are lower in elderly patients (Evers, p.1142), but this is not incorporated into the Marsh model.

stem: What does the 95% spectral edge frequency (SEF95) represent in processed EEG analysis?

options.A: The frequency below which 95% of the EEG amplitude lies
options.B: The frequency above which 95% of the EEG power lies
options.C: The frequency below which 95% of the EEG power lies
options.D: The frequency at which the peak EEG power occurs

reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

SEF95 is the frequency below which 95% of the total EEG power is contained. It is derived from the EEG power spectrum after Fourier analysis (Foundations of Anesthesia, p.164).

stem: Picture of an 8-second BIS monitor EEG trace with about 3 seconds of burst suppression. This most likely represents:
reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Burst suppression, with bursts of electrical activity alternating with near-isoelectric periods, occurs at deep levels of anaesthesia. BIS values below 40 are associated with burst suppression, whereas 40–60 is the usual general anaesthesia range (Kam & Power, p.91; Essentials of Anaesthetic Equipment, p.183). Therefore the best answer is deeply anaesthetised.

stem: A patient is in the lateral position. Blood pressure measured on the dependent arm is 120/80 mm Hg. The cuff on the non-dependent arm is 20 cm vertically above the cuff on the dependent arm. Assuming unchanged haemodynamics, what blood pressure would be measured on the non-dependent arm?
reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

A cuff 20 cm above the reference cuff reads 15.4 mm Hg lower because hydrostatic pressure changes by 7.7 mm Hg per 10 cm vertical height. Subtracting this from both systolic and diastolic pressures gives approximately 105/65 mm Hg. Dorsch & Dorsch, p.538.

stem: Which of these increases the risk of LA cardiac toxicity?
reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

Hypercarbia and its associated acidosis increase susceptibility to local anaesthetic systemic toxicity. Hypercarbia also raises plasma potassium, which facilitates depolarisation and markedly increases local anaesthetic toxicity; acidosis additionally depresses myocardial function. Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.307, describes increased PaCO2 lowering local anaesthetic toxicity thresholds and hyperkalaemia increasing toxicity.

stem: IV bolus of fentanyl. Dose doubled, which is correct:

options.A: Peak plasma concentration doubled, time to peak effect halved
options.B: Peak plasma concentration doubled, time to peak effect unchanged
options.C: Peak plasma concentration unchanged, time to peak effect halved
options.D: peak plasma concentration unchanged, time to peak effect unchanged

reason:
Answer and explanation supplied by the tracker's GPT audit (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-07 — not examiner-verified.

With linear pharmacokinetics, doubling an IV bolus doubles the plasma concentration at every time point, including the peak. It does not alter the disposition rate constants or effect-site equilibration constant, so the time to peak effect is unchanged. Stoelting p.44 identifies ke0 as the parameter governing effect-site delay and time to peak effect.
